summary: Provides a functional description of the signaling extensions needed for Generalized MPLS. GMPLS extends the MPLS control plane to time-division networks such as SONET and SDH, wavelength switching with optical lambdas, and spatial switching between ports or fibers.

eli5.summary: MPLS sets up paths for packets. GMPLS stretches that idea so it can set up paths on light colors and fibers too. This note describes what the signaling must do.

questions: what is a label set in gmpls
subtitle: How MPLS-style label signaling was stretched to set up paths over time slots, wavelengths and whole fibers.

tldr.problem: MPLS assumed every router could read packet or cell headers, but optical and TDM equipment forwards by time slot, wavelength or physical port and has no headers to read.
tldr.mechanism: Generalized MPLS defines a Generalized Label Request, a Generalized Label, label sets, bidirectional LSPs, protection and administrative status information, and a way to separate control and data channels. Protocol-specific encodings live in other documents.
tldr.outcome: This is the signaling-protocol-independent functional description. It is a Proposed Standard that has since been updated by several later RFCs.

facts.label: Bandwidth encoding
facts.value: 32-bit IEEE floating point, bytes per second

today: RFC 3471 is a Proposed Standard that has been updated by RFC 4201, RFC 4328, RFC 4872, RFC 6002, RFC 6003, RFC 6205, RFC 7074, RFC 7699 and RFC 8359, and it has not been obsoleted. It is the protocol-independent description; the wire formats are in RFC 3473 and RFC 3472.

sections.title: Why MPLS Needed Generalizing
sections.content:
MPLS assumes that a Label Switching Router (LSR) can recognize packet or cell boundaries and read a header to decide where to forward data. The architecture was then extended to LSRs whose forwarding plane recognizes neither packets nor cells, because they forward by time slot, wavelength or physical port.

The RFC sorts interfaces into four classes: Packet-Switch Capable (PSC), Time-Division Multiplex Capable (TDM), Lambda Switch Capable (LSC) and Fiber-Switch Capable (FSC). LSPs can nest in a hierarchy, with FSC at the top, then LSC, TDM and PSC. A packet LSP can ride inside a TDM LSP, which can ride inside a wavelength LSP, which can ride inside a fiber LSP.

The document is only a functional description. Protocol-specific formats are in RFC 3473 and RFC 3472, and technology-specific details are left to other documents.
sections.eli5: Some machines cannot read labels on packages. They only know which lane, color of light or cable something arrives on. GMPLS teaches label-style signaling to work for them too.

sections.title: What Changes from Traditional MPLS
sections.content:
Generalized MPLS adds support for TDM, lambda and fiber switching, and that touches basic LSP properties, how labels are requested and communicated, the one-way nature of LSPs, error propagation, and information for synchronizing the ingress and egress. An LSP must now start and end on the same type of LSR, and its payload can be something like SONET/SDH or 1 or 10Gb Ethernet.

Bandwidth on non-packet links can be allocated only in discrete units, and there are likely to be far fewer labels than on packet links. A Suggested Label lets an upstream node start configuring slow hardware, such as optical micro mirrors, early. A Label Set restricts which labels a downstream node may pick. Bidirectional LSPs, explicit label control, protection and administrative status information complete the list.

Technology-specific parameters are meant to ride in the RSVP SENDER_TSPEC and related objects, or in the CR-LDP Traffic Parameters TLV.
sections.eli5: Regular MPLS only has to handle parcels. GMPLS also has to handle things like beams of light, so it needs new ways to ask for a path, pick a lane, and carry traffic both ways.

sections.title: Label Request, Generalized Label and Label Sets
sections.content:
The Generalized Label Request carries three fields: an 8-bit LSP Encoding Type, an 8-bit Switching Type and a 16-bit G-PID. The encoding type describes the LSP itself, not the links it crosses (for example Packet is 1, Ethernet 2, SDH/SONET 5, Lambda 8, Fiber 9). The switching type names the kind of switching wanted on a link (PSC-1 to PSC-4 are 1 to 4, L2SC is 51, TDM 100, LSC 150, FSC 200). The G-PID identifies the client payload and is used by the LSP endpoints and sometimes the penultimate hop.

Bandwidth is a 32-bit IEEE floating point number in bytes per second, with guideline values for signals such as DS1, E1, STS-1, OC-48/STM-16 and 10GigE-LAN.

The Generalized Label has a variable-length label field whose meaning depends on the link. It can name a fiber in a bundle, a waveband, a wavelength or a set of time slots, and it has no type field because both ends know the link type from context. It carries one level of label only. A Waveband Label adds a 32-bit Waveband Id plus Start and End Labels for a contiguous group of wavelengths switched together.

A Label Set has an 8-bit Action (0 inclusive list, 1 exclusive list, 2 inclusive range, 3 exclusive range), a 14-bit Label Type and a list of subchannels. The receiver MUST choose from the set, and without a set any valid label may be used.
sections.eli5: When you ask for a path you say what kind of thing you will send, what kind of switching you want, and what is inside. The label then says which lane or color of light to use, and a label set is a list of lanes you may pick from.

sections.title: Bidirectional LSPs and Label Contention
sections.content:
Traditional RSVP-TE and CR-LDP LSPs are one-way, so a two-way connection needs two separate setups. The RFC lists the costs: extra setup latency, twice the control messages, harder route selection with possible races for resources, and awkward fit with SONET/SDH protection switching. It also notes that bidirectional optical LSPs are seen as a requirement by many optical service providers.

With GMPLS a single set of signaling messages sets up both directions. Two labels are allocated, and the presence of an Upstream Label object/TLV (same format as a generalized label) in the signaling message marks the LSP as bidirectional.

Two setups traveling in opposite directions can grab the same resources at the same time. To resolve the contention, the node with the higher node ID wins, and the other node MUST send a PathErr/NOTIFICATION with a Routing problem/Label allocation failure indication and SHOULD try a different upstream label. To make contention less likely, the lower-ID node can avoid suggesting labels, or the two sides can allocate from opposite ends of the label range.
sections.eli5: Two people may reach for the same seat on a train at the same moment. The rule is that the person with the bigger number keeps it, and the other one picks a different seat.

sections.title: Label Errors, Explicit Labels and Protection
sections.content:
When a node reports an "Unacceptable label value" error, it can now say which labels would work by sending an Acceptable Label Set, which has the same format as a Label Set.

A Label ERO subobject lets the initiator pick the exact label on a link, which an ordinary explicit route cannot do. It has an L bit that must be 0 and a U bit that is 1 for the upstream label on bidirectional LSPs. This helps, for example, when splicing the tail of one LSP into the head of another.

Protection Information is optional. It has an S bit marking a secondary (backup) LSP and a 6-bit Link Flags field. The flags are 0x20 Enhanced, 0x10 Dedicated 1+1, 0x08 Dedicated 1:1, 0x04 Shared, 0x02 Unprotected and 0x01 Extra Traffic. A value of 0 means any protection, including none, is fine. Resources of a secondary LSP may be used by other LSPs until the primary fails, and those LSPs MUST then be preempted.
sections.eli5: If a path request is turned down, the answer can include a list of choices that would be fine. You can also ask for a spare path that sits ready in case the main one breaks.

sections.title: Administrative Status and Control Channel Separation
sections.content:
Administrative Status Information is an optional object/TLV with four flags: R (reflect, asking the edge node to send the object back), T (testing), A (administratively down) and D (deletion in progress). It either reports the state of an LSP or requests that its state be changed, and a request is always relayed to the ingress node.

In traditional MPLS each control channel maps to one data channel. GMPLS allows them to be separate, for example when data channels cannot carry control traffic in-band. An Interface_ID object/TLV then identifies the data channel using an IPv4 address (type 1), an IPv6 address (type 2), an interface index (type 3) or a downstream or upstream component interface (types 4 and 5). The value 0xFFFFFFFF means the same label is valid across all component links.

Two new faults arise: a control channel failure while data keeps flowing, and a control plane restart that loses state. Both require neighbors to resynchronize state, and the details are left to RFC 3473 and RFC 3472.
sections.eli5: A control channel is like a phone line used to arrange deliveries, while the trucks drive on a different road. If the phone line breaks but the trucks keep moving, the two sides must compare notes afterwards.

sections.title: Security and IANA Considerations
sections.content:
The RFC introduces no new security considerations beyond RFC 3212 and RFC 3209. Those apply to the protocol-specific forms in RFC 3473 and RFC 3472.

IANA administers new values for the namespaces defined here: LSP Encoding Type (8 bits, 1 to 255, with 1 to 11 defined), Switching Type (8 bits, 1 to 255), Generalized PID (16 bits, 0 to 1500, with 0 to 46 defined), Action (8 bits, 0 to 3 defined) and Interface_ID Type (16 bits, 1 to 65535, with 1 to 5 defined). Future assignments go through IETF Consensus or a documented Specification.
sections.eli5: Nothing new needs locking down here, because the earlier protocols already cover it. A central office keeps the official list of numbers so nobody reuses one by accident.

fields.desc: Encoding of the LSP, such as Packet, SDH/SONET, Lambda or Fiber.

fields.name: Switching Type
fields.desc: Kind of switching wanted on a link, such as TDM, LSC or FSC.

fields.name: G-PID
fields.desc: Identifier of the client payload carried by the LSP.

fields.desc: Set to zero on transmission and ignored on receipt.

fields.desc: Desired link protection type; zero means any.
